item.title: Is photography failing us or can it save us? The power of context, perspective, and innovative curation…with Fred Ritchin | The War We See
item.description:
The War We See (2026-10-28)
I’m joined by the very inspirational Fred Ritchin, whose work has been at the forefront of debates about photography and its future for more than four decades. Fred is Dean Emeritus of the International Center of Photography in New York, a former picture editor of the New York Times Magazine, and the author of several groundbreaking books, including After Photography, Bending the Frame, and, most recently, The Synthetic Eye: Photography Transformed in the Age of AI.
In this fascinating and thought-provoking conversation, Fred reflects on his long relationship with the medium of photography and photojournalism, particularly the significance of editorial choices in shaping how photographs are understood, and the importance of context for responsibly producing and disseminating images. We explore his longstanding argument that photography has struggled to adapt to the possibilities offered by new technologies, discussing his many innovative projects over the years, like Pixel Press, the Four Corners Project, and his most recent platform, The Fifth Corner, and the need to develop more creative and credible approaches to visual storytelling. We also consider the challenges and opportunities presented by AI-generated imagery, and how these emerging technologies might be used in ways that better serve society.

item.title: Gary Knight: nobody wins a war | The Eyeshot Podcast on Street & Documentary Photography
item.description:
The Eyeshot Podcast on Street & Documentary Photography (2026-09-11)
Gary Knight on war, evidence, and the limits of what a photographer can know. In this Eyeshot 50mm conversation the British photojournalist, co-founder of VII Photo Agency and Executive Director of The VII Foundation, explains why nobody wins a war, why he no longer needs to be the one telling other people's stories, and why he believes photojournalism has to be liberated from the press. Four decades inside conflict, from Cambodia to Bosnia, Kosovo, Iraq and Afghanistan. He is harder on his own work than on anyone else's: he calls what he made in Bosnia superficial, and says that four decades in, he trusts his own certainty less than he did at the start. He talks about the ethics of proximity and the gift handed to you by the people who let you in, about founding VII on a shoestring in September 2001, about The Stringer and what happens when journalists face the questions they spend their lives asking everybody else, and about the grieving mother photograph we have all seen too many times. Gary Knight co-founded VII Photo Agency on 9 September 2001. He is Executive Director and co-founder of The VII Foundation, which runs the VII Academy and its education programmes for photographers from the majority world. Interview © Eyeshot. Gary Knight appears courtesy of The VII Foundation. Watch the full video interview on YouTube. https://youtu.be/bbTeIWcX5ZQ

item.title: Nadya Bair, "The Decisive Network: Magnum Photos and the Postwar Image Market" (U California Press, 2020) | New Books in Photography
item.description:
New Books in Photography (2021-07-20)
The legendary Magnum photo agency has long been associated with heroic lone wolf male photographers such as Frank Capa and Henri Cartier-Bresson, roaming the world in search of the “decisive moment” – the perfect shot that captured the essence of a major news story. Nadya Bair’s highly original book The Decisive Network: Magnum Photos and the Postwar Image Market (University of California Press 2020) argues that this idealized portrayal of Magnum occludes the larger networks within which these photographers operated, including the crucial roles performed by often female office staff, by picture editors and corporate clients. She sets out to show that right from the outset, Magnum was also a business operation, one that pioneered modern ideas of branding borrowed from advertising agencies and commercial partners. Drawing on extensive archival work and including numerous images of photo page spreads, The Decisive Network presents Magnum in a novel and distinctive light, as the framer of new global imaginaries that reflected the evolution of post-war capitalism. Nadya Bair is an assistant professor of art history at Hamilton College For digital explorations of the Magnum network, see Nadya’s fascinating website. ﻿Duncan McCargo is an eclectic, internationalist political scientist and literature buff: his day job is directing the Nordic Institute of Asian Studies at the University of Copenhagen. Learn more here, here, here, and here. Support our show by becoming a premium member!

item.title: Don McCullin | This Cultural Life
item.description:
This Cultural Life (2026-04-09)
Award-winning photographer Sir Don McCullin talks to John Wilson about his cultural influences and formative experiences. He started out in the late 1950s documenting the working-class lives in the north London neighbourhood in which he had grown up. Employed by the Observer newspaper, and later the Sunday Times, McCullin photographs captured scenes of struggle, despair and violence. Travelling to the front lines of conflict zones in Cyprus, Beirut, Vietnam, Cambodia, Biafra, Northern Ireland and elsewhere, McCullin earned a hard-won reputation as one of the greatest war photographers of all time. In recent years he has focused his lens on the beauty of the natural world, particularly the landscape around his home in Somerset. His work is held in permanent collections around the world including the Tate, the National Portrait Gallery and the V&A. He was knighted in 2017 for services to photography. Producer: Edwina Pitman

item.title: Joel Meyerowitz | This Cultural Life
item.description:
This Cultural Life (2026-09-24)
American photographer Joel Meyerowitz talks to John Wilson about his cultural influences and formative experiences. A pioneer of the artform, he first began capturing life on the streets of his native New York in the early 1960s, and helped to establish colour photography as a fine-art medium. After travelling throughout Europe he made his name with a groundbreaking show at the Museum of Modern Art in 1968. Following the attacks on the World Trade Centre in 2001, Joel Meyerowitz became the only photographer to secure access to Ground Zero and, over several months, captured the scenes of devastation. His work has been the subject of more than 350 exhibitions in museums and galleries around the world, and he is the recipient of many awards, most recently the prestigious Outstanding Contribution prize at the Sony World Photography Awards 2026. Producer: Edwina Pitman

item.title: Spanish Civil War & Gerda Taro | Warfare
item.description:
Warfare (Fri, 16 Ju) Starting off as a novice photographer with strong political motivations, Gerda Taro became well known during the Spanish Civil War, only to sadly become the first woman photojournalist to have died covering the frontline of a war, aged 26. In this episode, Jane Rogoyska joins James to talk us through Gerda’s background, her partnership with her fellow photojournalist, known as Robert Capa, and her experience of the Spanish Civil War. Jane is a writer and film-maker who has been discovering the truth about Gerda Taro.

Hosted on Acast. See acast.com/privacy for more information.
